findings.title: Ignored providers are still instantiated and mutate global JCA state
findings.body:
`detectProvider` now iterates the whole `ServiceLoader` and sorts the results. That instantiates every `CryptoProvider` on the classpath, including the ones that end up ignored. These constructors have global side effects:
- `FIPS1402Provider` calls `Security.insertProviderAt` to put KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3, and changes the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory security properties.
- `DefaultCryptoProvider` registers BouncyCastle.

Before this change, having several providers on the classpath was a hard error, so the side effects could not go unnoticed. Now a provider that is 'ignored' (only reported in a debug log) can still reorder JVM security providers and TLS defaults. Ordering should be resolved without instantiating every provider, for example via `ServiceLoader.stream()` or a static order, or the side effects should be moved out of the constructors.

findings.title: Equal-order providers now resolve silently and nondeterministically
findings.body: `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200. If two of them are on the classpath (e.g. FIPS plus default), selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration, which is effectively classpath order. Previously this case threw an `IllegalStateException`. Now it only logs at debug level. As a result, a deployment intended to run in FIPS mode could silently pick the non-FIPS provider. Keep failing when more than one provider shares the highest order, or give the providers distinct orders.

findings.title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation (custom crypto providers, older keycloak-client copies) will fail to compile. Already-compiled implementations will hit `AbstractMethodError` when `detectProvider` calls `order()`. A `default` method returning a neutral value would preserve compatibility.

findings.title: Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies the re-encoded DER
findings.body: The key pair is generated with the default EC size (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512. As a result, r and s are always about 32 bytes, and the 48- and 66-byte cases (including P-521 values with leading bytes) are never exercised. The test also only checks that DER -> RS -> DER -> RS round-trips to the same RS. It never checks that the produced DER is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it matches the existing BC implementation, so a symmetric encoding bug would pass. Use curve-appropriate keys (secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the reconstructed DER signature.

findings.title: Dead code: encoders created and discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write the r and s integers into them, and then discard the results. The real encoding is done again on lines 117-121. These two lines do nothing except allocate, and they should be removed.
